37: Whether the mark NOPALEA is merely descriptive of nutritional supplements containing nopal juice under Section 2(e)(1), so as not to be registrable absent secondary meaning.
We affirm the Board's decision that NOPALEA is not registrable on the Principal Register for TriVita's nutritional supplements containing nopal juice.
422: Genericness and mere descriptiveness of the COLORWORX mark; Board granted summary judgment and the court affirmed because Beling produced no evidence of how the public understands the mark as a whole.

Because Mr. Beling failed to produce evidence of how the relevant public would understand Ennis's mark as a whole, we agree with the Board that Mr. Beling failed to create a genuine issue of material fact as to whether Ennis's mark is generic or merely descriptive.
489: Whether FISH FRY PRODUCTS has acquired distinctiveness, so that the PTO could require a disclaimer of that term in the applied-for composite mark; the court affirmed the finding that the applicant failed to carry its burden.
substantial evidence supports the Board's determination that Louisiana Fish Fry failed to show that FISH FRY PRODUCTS has acquired distinctiveness.
1070: Whether the term EMPORIUM is merely descriptive of video/amusement arcade and bar services, requiring a disclaimer; Board found it descriptive and court affirmed under substantial evidence review.
We agree with the PTO that substantial evidence supports the Board's determinations.
1719: Acquired distinctiveness under Section 2(f): the Board rejected the claim because the years of use were not trademark use and there was no evidence the matter was promoted as a trademark.
we cannot find that the applied-for mark has acquired distinctiveness regardless of the time the applied-for mark has been used in this manner.
1798: Genericness of CHURRASCOS for restaurant services: the Board's finding that the term is generic, with the burden of proof and substantial-evidence review, so the mark is not registrable.
We affirm the TTAB's decision that the stylized form of CHURRASCOS applied for in the '191 Application is generic as applied to restaurant services and therefore trademark-ineligible.
1799: Whether the stylization of the mark makes it registrable apart from the generic word; held that the stylization cannot save the mark from ineligibility as generic.
The stylized nature of the mark cannot save it from ineligibility as generic.
3256: Whether the mark FIRST TUESDAY is merely descriptive (not registrable absent secondary meaning) or suggestive (inherently distinctive); court held substantial evidence supports TTAB finding of mere descriptiveness, considering explanatory text in specimens.
On the record of this case, we agree with the PTO that substantial evidence supports the TTAB's finding of mere descriptiveness.
3387: Whether the DOTBLOG mark is merely descriptive (not registrable under §2(e)(1)) or suggestive of the applicant's information services; court held the mark suggestive and not descriptive.
When considering DOTBLOG within the context of Driven Innovations' proffered services, we find the mark merely suggestive of those services.
3401: Genericness of MAGNESITA for Class 19 refractory products (doctrine of foreign equivalents; generic for the genus), so the mark is not registrable on the Supplemental Register.
Because we affirm the Board's finding that MAGNESITA is generic for the genus of refractory products set forth in MRC's application, it cannot be registered as a trademark.
3402: Acquired distinctiveness under §2(f) for Class 37 services, where the mark is highly descriptive and the applicant's sales data and five years of use were not enough without evidence of public perception.
Thus, absent a showing of acquired distinctiveness, MRC cannot register MAGNESITA as a trademark.
3588: Genericness of PRETZEL CRISPS for pretzel crackers. The Board applied the wrong legal standard by analyzing the compound term's constituent words instead of the mark as a whole under Marvin Ginn. The court vacated the genericness finding and remanded without deciding registrability.

Because the Board applied the incorrect legal standard in assessing whether the term PRETZEL CRISPS is generic, we vacate the Board's decision cancelling Registration No. 2,980,303 and its decision sustaining Frito-Lay's opposition to Application Serial No. 76/700,802.
3935: Genericness of ZERO in combination beverage marks. The Board applied the wrong legal framing by not examining whether ZERO refers to a key aspect or sub-group of the claimed beverage genus, and it improperly treated sales and advertising figures as bearing on genericness. Vacated and remanded.
The Board asked the wrong question in assessing the alleged genericness of the ZERO term.
3936: Acquired distinctiveness of ZERO under Section 2(f). The Board failed to first determine the level of descriptiveness of the mark and did not assess the survey and other evidence through the exacting lens required for highly descriptive marks. Vacated and remanded.
the Board should have first assessed the level of the marks' descriptiveness before determining whether TCCC satisfied its burden of establishing acquired distinctiveness.
4128: Secondary meaning of the trade dress mark: ITC applied the wrong standard and must make a specific secondary-meaning determination as of the relevant date; vacated and remanded.
Because the relevant date is so important to the secondary-meaning analysis, we find that a specific determination of secondary meaning as of the relevant date must be made.
4129: Presumption of secondary meaning from registration does not apply to infringement that began before registration; Converse must prove secondary meaning without the presumption for pre-registration uses.

We conclude that Converse's registration confers a presumption of secondary meaning beginning only as of the date of registration and confers no presumption of secondary meaning before the date of registration.
4874: Whether the mark BREW SCIENCE is merely descriptive of the identified entertainment services (descriptiveness refusal under 15 U.S.C. §1052(e)(1)); Board finding of mere descriptiveness affirmed under substantial evidence review.
Because substantial evidence supports the Board's conclusion, we affirm.
4884: Mark CORN THINS and RICE THINS held merely descriptive under the Lanham Act; the TTAB's descriptiveness finding is supported by substantial evidence and affirmed.
Substantial evidence supports the TTAB's descriptiveness finding.
4885: Marks have not acquired distinctiveness (secondary meaning); the TTAB's finding is supported by substantial evidence and affirmed.
Substantial evidence supports the TTAB's finding that Real Foods' proposed, highly descriptive marks have not acquired distinctiveness.
4886: Frito-Lay's genericness claim: the TTAB improperly narrowed the genus of goods to popped corn cakes and rice cakes, ignoring that these are types of crispbread/crackers; the genericness dismissal is vacated and remanded for reconsideration under the correct genus.
This was error. As set forth in Real Foods' Applications and the Motion to Amend, see J.A. 279, corn cakes and rice cakes are the species, not the genus
5622: Acquired distinctiveness under Section 2(f): the Board found applicant failed to prove the designs acquired distinctiveness; the court did not reach this issue.
Because substantial evidence supports the Board's functionality determination, we need not reach acquired distinctiveness.
5932: Inherent distinctiveness of color-based product packaging mark; Board erred in requiring a well-defined peripheral shape or border for inherent distinctiveness
To the extent the Board's decision suggests that a multi-color mark must be associated with a specific peripheral shape in order to be inherently distinctive, that too, was error.
6405: Acquired distinctiveness under Section 2(f): Board found SCHLAFLY word mark for beer had acquired secondary meaning based on use evidence, without survey evidence; affirmed.
The Board and courts have recognized that both direct and circumstantial evidence may show secondary meaning.
6599: Whether the mark THE JOINT is merely descriptive of restaurant, bar, nightclub and entertainment services under Section 2(e)(1), and whether applicant established acquired distinctiveness under Section 2(f)

We conclude that substantial evidence supports the Board's conclusions that THE JOINT is merely descriptive of JC Hospitality's services and that JC Hospitality has not demonstrated acquired distinctiveness.
11015: Secondary meaning / acquired distinctiveness of registered product-configuration trade dress; the court affirmed that the registration's presumption of validity stood and that SoClean was likely to defeat Sunset's lack-of-secondary-meaning defense.
Accordingly, we affirm the district court's finding that SoClean is likely to defeat Sunset's secondary meaning defense.
11069: Whether the registered BROOKLYN BREW SHOP mark is merely descriptive under Section 2(e)(1); Brewery failed to rebut the presumption of inherent distinctiveness.
We therefore find the Board's conclusion that the presumption of inherent distinctiveness as to the registered mark was not overcome is supported by substantial evidence.
11435: Inherent distinctiveness of ALL RISE and HERE COMES THE JUDGE as arbitrary marks; surname and nickname arguments rejected
Again, we agree with the Board.
11954: Genericness of KAHWA for cafés and coffee shops: court held the Board's genericness finding unsupported by substantial evidence because no record evidence shows cafés sell kahwa.
Accordingly, the Board's finding that relevant customers would understand KAHWA to be generic for cafés and coffee shops is not supported by substantial evidence.
11955: Mere descriptiveness of KAHWA for cafés and coffee shops: court held the Board's descriptiveness finding unsupported by substantial evidence, so the mark is not merely descriptive.
Accordingly, the Board's finding that relevant customers would understand KAHWA to be merely descriptive for cafés and coffee shops is not supported by substantial evidence.
12268: Whether Heritage's iVoterGuide marks are merely descriptive or highly descriptive, and so not inherently distinctive and not registrable as a basis for priority
We thus see no reason to disturb the Board's finding that the iVoterGuide marks are highly descriptive.
12269: Whether the iVoterGuide marks had acquired distinctiveness (secondary meaning) by January 22, 2019, including the weight given to five years of use under 15 U.S.C. § 1052(f) and volunteer declarations
We conclude that the Board's determination that the marks had not acquired distinctiveness by January 2019 is supported by substantial evidence.
13014: Whether the applied-for mark YUCATAN SHRIMP is merely descriptive under Lanham Act 2(e)(1) and thus not registrable; Board finding of descriptiveness upheld under substantial evidence.
Substantial evidence supports the Board's conclusion that the YUCATAN SHRIMP mark is merely descriptive of Mr. White's goods.
13948: Genericness of FIREBALL: whether the FIREBALL marks were generic at the times of registration, with the court holding the proper time for assessing genericness is the time of registration and affirming the Board's finding of no genericness under substantial evidence review.
Because the Board did not err in finding FIREBALL was not generic at the time of registration and determining there is no likelihood of confusion between FIREBALL and BULLSHINE FIREBULL, we affirm.
14373: Whether the proposed mark FORMULARYHUB is merely descriptive of Agadia's software services under 15 U.S.C. § 1052(e)(1); Board found it descriptive and the court found substantial evidence supported that finding.

Finally, the Board concluded that the words “formulary” and “hub” separately, as well as the proposed mark FORMULARYHUB in its entirety, are merely descriptive. Id. at *8. This is substantial evidence.
14981: Genericness and, alternatively, mere descriptiveness without acquired distinctiveness of the proposed mark MODULAR GABION SYSTEMS for gabions of steel wire; the Board's refusal to register was affirmed under substantial evidence review.
Substantial evidence supports the Board's conclusion that the proposed mark is generic.
14989: Genericness of a dark green color mark for chloroprene medical examination gloves. The court adopted the Milwaukee two-step test for color marks, held the Board applied the correct standard, and held substantial evidence supported the finding that the mark is generic and ineligible for either register.
Applying the Milwaukee test, we conclude that substantial evidence supports the Board's determination that Medisafe's proposed color mark is generic.
15215: Genericness of VETEMENTS marks (translated as clothing) for clothing and retail services; mark generic and not registrable
Substantial evidence supports the Board's finding that, as translated to "clothing," the marks are generic.
